title: AI That Answers Without a Round Trip to a Server
description: Eight tools that keep the work on your machine or cut the round trips: offline libraries, VRAM maths, local widgets, co-op inference and video.
tldr: Survival LLM is a free offline assistant and emergency library that cites the passage it read, Run LLM Locally tells you which model actually fits your GPU, and Chopstick turns a local activity log into Mac widgets your own agent builds. Inference Cooperative sells open-weights inference through a co-op, Visible by AI runs 16 crawlability checks, Saanora answers as diagrams and 3D models, and AIVideosUGC and TensorPix cover brand video from one photo or from footage you already have.
content:
# AI That Answers Without a Round Trip to a Server

Not every launch this week was an agent framework. This group is about distance: how far the request has to travel, and how much of the answer can be produced before anything leaves the machine. Some of these remove the network entirely, some just remove a wasted trip, and one of them is about the trip your website takes when a crawler comes looking.

## An assistant that works in a blackout

[[link:/tools/2194|Survival LLM]] is a free, open-source AI assistant and emergency library that runs entirely on your own computer and needs no internet after setup. Ask how to keep food safe during a power cut, how to treat a burn or how to purify water, and it answers from a bundled library of medical references, FEMA and CDC guidance, survival manuals, how-to and repair guides and roughly 930,000 Wikipedia articles. The part that makes it trustworthy rather than merely offline is that every answer lists the articles it read, and you can click through to the exact passage highlighted. On first run the app checks your memory and downloads the model that fits, from IBM Granite 4.2 8B on a 16 GB machine up to NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super on a 128 GB Mac. The library itself is a 9 GB download, about 19 GB installed.

## Does it actually fit

Before you download anything, [[link:/tools/2204|Run LLM Locally]] answers the question that decides the whole exercise: which local models will your GPU or Mac run, how much memory does each need at each quantization, and roughly how many tokens per second should you expect. It works in both directions, so you can name a model and be shown the hardware it needs, or ask it to build you a compatible PC or Mac configuration around a target. The card list covers NVIDIA, AMD and Intel parts plus Apple Silicon, and it is free. The speed figures are estimates rather than benchmarks on your machine, which is the right level of honesty for a planner.

## Widgets written by the agent you already pay for

[[link:/tools/2193|Chopstick]] watches what you repeat on your Mac and builds notch widgets for it, using the coding agent you already have, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot or OpenCode. The activity log stays local and shows active time, longest focus stretch, app switches, keystrokes and a timeline of the day. You can start from the widgets it already ships with or describe your own and let the agent build it. It is a paid app at a $14.99 launch price with a three-day trial, macOS 15 or later, and the sensible thing about it is that it does not run its own model, it uses yours.

## Inference as a cooperative

[[link:/tools/2203|Inference Cooperative]] is the odd one out and the most interesting governance experiment in the batch. It is a member-governed cooperative for AI inference: members choose among powerful open-weights models and pick by the values they care about, with options for models running in encrypted enclaves so even the cooperative cannot read your prompts, and models served on 100% renewable power. One membership opens the chat, the developer API and a seat in governance. Dues are a sliding scale from $5 a month and every member gets the same $15 monthly credit regardless of what they paid. Credits never expire and carry over. Pricing itself is a co-op decision, which is a sentence you rarely get to write about a cloud service.

## What a crawler sees when it arrives

The round trip worth worrying about for most sites is not the model call, it is the crawl. [[link:/tools/2190|Visible by AI Checker]] runs 16 AI-visibility checks over HTTPS and returns a score plus the fixes that matter: schema, robots.txt, AI crawler access, llms.txt and answer formatting. It reads your homepage as a server-rendered document plus those three files, four requests in total, with no signup, no email and no stored results. It is honest about the limit, it cannot execute JavaScript, so anything rendered on the client is invisible to it, and it does not predict where you will rank or be cited.

## One assistant, and answers that are not paragraphs

[[link:/tools/2209|Saanora]] is a single assistant built around a chat called Mark that answers, researches the web, writes and codes in more than 20 languages. Where it differs from another chat wrapper is the shape of the answer: diagrams, quizzes and 3D models where those are clearer than prose. It reasons through the request, cites its sources, and remembers you across chats, so the context does not reset every time you open a new tab.

## A listing video from one photo

[[link:/tools/2191|AIVideosUGC]] is built for brands, agencies and creators: animate one product photo into a short clip, paste a product link and get a video, or turn a written brief into an editable plan. Alongside it sit white-background, lifestyle and model product photography, 18 templates and 53 AI actors, with downloads sized for Meta or TikTok and no watermark. Templates are grouped by industry, platform and occasion, which is efficient and also the reason these outputs tend to look alike.

## Rescue the footage you already have

[[link:/tools/2205|TensorPix]] works on the material you already shot. The headline use case turns property photos into walkthrough videos in minutes, but the same account covers a video enhancer, TensorShots, an AI video generator, an AI image generator and a video compressor, with use cases spanning call enhancement, restoration, frame interpolation, unblurring, stabilising, denoising and upscaling, including AI-generated video and anime. Three videos are free with no card required, and an API runs the same jobs without a person clicking through an editor.

## Where the work happens

Strip these down and there is one argument running through all eight: put the work where the constraint is. If the constraint is connectivity, ship the library to the machine. If it is memory, do the arithmetic before the download. If it is privacy, run in an enclave or not at all. If it is money, reuse instead of regenerating. The tools that get this right stop feeling like AI products and start feeling like software that happens to have a model in it, which is probably the direction the whole category is heading.
